sections.history: Uraiyur, now a quarter of Tiruchirappalli, was the capital of the early Cholas, a city whose fame reached ancient writers abroad long before the Tevaram was sung. In the hymns of Sambandar the Shiva temple here is Tirumukkeecharam, and it is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the southern bank of the Kaveri. Chola-period inscriptions record gifts to the shrine, among them the grant of a village for its upkeep, and the temple seen today carries the work of medieval patrons and later renovators. The town is also remembered as Kozhiyur, the town of the cock, a name that preserves its founding legend, and it has remained a place of Shaiva worship through every change of ruler.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a five-tiered rajagopuram and is laid out in three enclosures in the Dravidian manner, with the older stone core ringed by later construction. At the entrance to the sanctum stand finely carved dvarapalas, guardian figures that some sources assign to the eighth century, and the niches of the sanctum wall hold images of Brahma, Vishnu and Durga. Within the sanctum Panchavarneswarar is worshipped as a linga, while the goddess Kanthimathi Ammai has her own shrine in the enclosure. The sacred Naga Theertham recalls the serpent-king's daughters of the temple's legend.
sections.legends: The temple takes its name from the Lord of five colours. The sage Uthanga is said to have beheld Shiva here in five different hues through the five periods of a single day, and so the deity is Panchavarneswarar. A second tradition tells of Nagaraja, the serpent king, whose five daughters each worshipped a linga on the bank of the sacred tank; a Chola king who saw them married the youngest, and the lingas were joined into one, the Lord who now stands in the sanctum. A third story explains the town's older name, Kozhiyur. A Chola king was riding an elephant that grew maddened, until a brave cock struck its forehead and turned it back; moved by such courage in so small a creature, the king made this place his capital. Most tellings name him Karikalan, while another names Veeravathithan, and the accounts differ in their details.
sections.festivals: The principal festival is the Vaikasi Brahmotsavam, held in May or June, which commemorates the lingas merging into one. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and the festivals of the Shaiva year are kept with devotion. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Uraiyur suits an unhurried visit. Enter beneath the five-tiered gopuram, come to the sanctum of Panchavarneswarar, and then turn to the goddess Kanthimathi Ammai in her own shrine. It is a pleasure to walk the enclosures with the old stories in mind: the Lord seen in five colours, the serpent king's daughters at the tank, the courage of the cock. The Vaishnava temple of Azhagiya Manavala Perumal stands a short way off, and the temple pairs naturally with the Thayumanavar shrine on the Rockfort in a single day. Though the quarter is busy with city traffic, the temple keeps its quiet within the walls.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from the afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is customary: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer enclosures but not inside the sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple practice. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Uraiyur is a quarter of Tiruchirappalli city, a few kilometres from the centre, and is easily reached from the Chatram bus stand by city bus or auto-rickshaw. Tiruchirappalli Junction is the main railway station, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport lies on the southern side of the city. The Azhagiya Manavala Perumal temple is a few hundred metres away.
